newsitem.title: GREECE: Athens fetes socialism with fireworks, champagne.
newsitem.headline: Athens fetes socialism with fireworks, champagne.

text.p: Thousands of Greek socialist party supporters threw a big party in Athens on Sunday, blaring car horns and waving green flags to celebrate the election victory of Prime Minister Costas Simitis and his PASOK party.

Champagne flowed at party headquarters in central Athens until well after midnight and a cheering crowd gave the smiling Simitis a hero's welcome as he entered the building to prepare his victory speech.
"Simitis took the risk and won. It is a victory for the people, it is a victory which says Greece is socialist and will remain socialist," said Valerios Kahrimakis, a PASOK voter.
"We dedicate this night to our (late party) founder Andreas Papandreou. Wherever he is, he is proud of us," he added.

PASOK officials threw red roses and carnations, symbols of socialism, to the crowd. Delivery boys struggled through with big boxes of chocolates sent by PASOK offices from around the country and loudspeakers blared bouzouki (traditional music).

The central Omonia square, with the famous Acropolis ancient Greek monument in the background, was also packed by a jubilant crowd who danced to the sounds of folk music and set off fireworks to light up the night sky.

The celebrations brought back memories of previous PASOK wins in 1981, 1985 and 1993, when hundreds of thousands took to the streets hailing the fiery Papandreou who mesmerised them with passionate speeches.

But following his death in June, PASOK seemed numbed and this campaign was mostly dominated by television debates rather than mass rallies and a feeling that the Greek passion for politics ended with the veteran leader.
"This is a night of victory," said Costas Laliotis, Simitis's Environment Minister and PASOK's campaign manager since 1977. "The glory days have returned."
First official results showed PASOK leading the conservative New Democracy party by three points and poll officials said the vote trend was irreversible.
Across town, in the New Democracy headquarters, only a few dozen depressed-looking people waited outside, arguing what went wrong and expressing concern over the future of New Democracy.

Stands with wine and sweets that were put up earlier in the day to treat voters soon disappeared and gloomy party leader Miltiades Evert waved to his few supporters as he left to announce his resignation.
"I personally undertake the responsibility for my party's defeat. I resign from the presidency of New Democracy," he told reporters at Zappeion Hall, the main election press centre.

The sober mood at New Democracy headquarters was briefly disrupted by a newly-wed couple passing by in a convertible blaring its horn. "Life goes on," Yannis Apostolides, a conservative voter said. "New Democracy will find its way back to the top with a new leader."
